$comment: themob weakness pack: the canonical identities findings are keyed by. Adapters reference 'key', never a tool's own rule name, or two tools reporting the same weakness will not merge and cross-tool voting never fires. mobile_top10 carries the OWASP Mobile Top 10 (2024) category. maswe_id is still null on purpose: the MAS Weakness Enumeration ids could not be verified against the OWASP source from here, and a wrong standards reference in a pentest report is worse than a missing one. Fill them from https://mas.owasp.org/MASWE/ and the loader will carry them through with no code change.

weaknesses.title: Application is debuggable
weaknesses.description: android:debuggable is true in the shipped manifest. Anyone who can install the package can attach a debugger, read and rewrite process memory, and call into any method regardless of visibility, which collapses every client-side control the app relies on.
weaknesses.remediation: Remove android:debuggable from the manifest and let the build type set it. A release build must never ship with it true.

weaknesses.title: Application data can be backed up
weaknesses.description: android:allowBackup is true (or left at its default), so the app's private data can be extracted over ADB or through cloud backup without root, including any credentials or tokens it keeps in its own sandbox.
weaknesses.remediation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or define a backup rules file that excludes every store holding credentials or personal data.

weaknesses.title: Cleartext traffic is permitted
weaknesses.description: The app permits plain HTTP. Anyone on the network path can read and modify the traffic, and an attacker who can answer DNS can serve their own responses.
weaknesses.remediation: Set android:usesCleartextTraffic="false" and declare a network security config with cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"; move any remaining HTTP endpoint to TLS.

weaknesses.title: Cleartext traffic is permitted for specific domains
weaknesses.description: A domain-scoped network security config entry permits cleartext. Narrower than a global opt-in, but traffic to those hosts is still readable and modifiable in transit.
weaknesses.remediation: Remove the domain override and serve the host over TLS. If it is a development host, keep the override in a debug-only manifest.

weaknesses.title: User-installed CAs are trusted
weaknesses.description: The network security config trusts the "user" certificate store, so any certificate the device owner installs is accepted. That is what makes casual traffic interception possible on an unrooted device, and it is rarely what a release build wants.
weaknesses.remediation: Trust only the "system" anchor in the release configuration; keep the user store in a debug-overrides block if testing needs it.

weaknesses.title: No network security config on a target SDK that allows cleartext
weaknesses.description: The app declares no network security config and targets an SDK below 28, where the platform default permits cleartext. The app is therefore free to make plain-HTTP requests whether or not it currently does.
weaknesses.remediation: Add a network security config with cleartextTrafficPermitted set to false, and raise targetSdkVersion to 28 or above.

weaknesses.title: Component is exported without a permission
weaknesses.description: The component is reachable from any other app on the device and enforces no permission. Whatever it does on receiving an Intent, it does for an arbitrary caller.
weaknesses.remediation: Set android:exported="false" if no other app needs it. If it must stay exported, guard it with a signature-level permission and validate every field of the incoming Intent.

weaknesses.title: Content provider is exported without a permission
weaknesses.description: An exported provider with no read or write permission exposes its backing store to every app on the device. Unlike an exported activity, the default reachable surface here is data, and a provider that concatenates its selection is also an injection target.
weaknesses.remediation: Set android:exported="false", or declare readPermission and writePermission and restrict the exposed URIs with path permissions and grant-URI rules.

weaknesses.title: Custom permission uses a weak protection level
weaknesses.description: A permission the app defines is declared normal or dangerous rather than signature. A normal permission is granted to any app that asks, so guarding a component with it is close to not guarding it; a dangerous one is granted by a user prompt an attacker's app can also obtain.
weaknesses.remediation: Use android:protectionLevel="signature" for permissions that only the app's own components, or its own suite, should hold.

weaknesses.title: Minimum SDK is below a maintained Android release
weaknesses.description: The app installs on Android versions that no longer receive security patches, and it silently loses the platform hardening newer releases provide.
weaknesses.remediation: Raise minSdkVersion to a maintained release and drop the compatibility paths that only existed for older ones.

weaknesses.title: Package is signed with the v1 scheme only
weaknesses.description: Only the JAR-based v1 signature is present. v1 signs entries rather than the archive, which is what the Janus class of attacks abuses, and it leaves the rest of the container unauthenticated.
weaknesses.remediation: Sign with APK Signature Scheme v2 or later (v3 for key rotation) in addition to, or instead of, v1.

weaknesses.title: Private key is embedded in the package
weaknesses.description: A private key is shipped inside the application package. Every installation carries the same key, so recovering it once compromises it everywhere, and the app has no way to rotate it without a release.
weaknesses.remediation: Remove the key from the package. Keep private keys server-side, or generate a per-device key in the Android Keystore where the material cannot be extracted.

weaknesses.title: Cloud provider credential is hardcoded
weaknesses.description: A credential for a cloud provider is embedded in the package. Anyone who unpacks the app holds whatever that credential is entitled to, and the entitlement is usually far wider than the one call the app makes.
weaknesses.remediation: Revoke the credential, then move the call behind a backend the app authenticates to. If the app must talk to the provider directly, use short-lived scoped tokens issued at runtime.

weaknesses.title: Third-party service API key is hardcoded
weaknesses.description: An API key for a third-party service is embedded in the package. What it costs depends on the service: some keys are public by design, others bill the account or read customer data, so each one needs checking rather than assuming.
weaknesses.remediation: Rotate the key. Decide per service whether it is safe to ship: if it authorises anything billable or private, proxy the call through a backend instead.

weaknesses.title: High-entropy string that looks like a secret
weaknesses.description: A string matched a generic secret pattern rather than a known provider format. These are the noisy ones: a build hash or a test fixture looks the same to a scanner, so this needs a human before it goes in a report.
weaknesses.remediation: Confirm what the string is. If it authenticates anything, rotate it and move it out of the package; if it does not, mark the finding as a false positive so it stops recurring.

weaknesses.title: Cipher used in a mode that leaks plaintext structure
weaknesses.description: The app requests a block cipher in ECB mode, or in a mode with no integrity protection. ECB encrypts identical plaintext blocks to identical ciphertext blocks, so structure survives encryption and an attacker can often recover or rearrange content without ever breaking the key.
weaknesses.remediation: Use an authenticated mode, AES-GCM for new code. If a mode without integrity is unavoidable, pair it with a separate MAC over the ciphertext and never reuse a nonce.

weaknesses.title: Broken hash function in use
weaknesses.description: The app requests MD5 or SHA-1. Both have practical collision attacks, so neither can support a signature, an integrity check or a deduplication key that an attacker has any reason to subvert. Whether it matters here depends on what the digest is used for, which is worth checking rather than assuming.
weaknesses.remediation: Use SHA-256 or better for integrity. For passwords use a memory-hard KDF such as Argon2 or scrypt, never a bare hash of any kind.

weaknesses.title: Bundled library has a known vulnerability
weaknesses.description: A library compiled into the package has a published advisory against the exact version bundled. The app ships that code whether or not it calls the affected function, so the question for a tester is reachability, not presence.
weaknesses.remediation: Upgrade to the fixed version named in the advisory. Where no fix exists, confirm whether the vulnerable path is reachable from the app's own code before accepting the risk.

weaknesses.title: Backend endpoint addressed over plain HTTP
weaknesses.description: The app carries a plain-HTTP URL for a backend it talks to. This is stronger evidence than a permissive network policy: the policy says cleartext is allowed, this says the app actually addresses a host that way. Anyone on the network path can read and rewrite that traffic, and whoever answers the DNS query decides what the app receives.
weaknesses.remediation: Move the endpoint to TLS and change the URL. Removing the cleartext permission without changing the URL turns a silent interception into an outage, so change both.
